What the documents show

Six findings, each measured across all 2,835 resolutions and every recorded vote.

The Council went from recommending to ordering"Decides" appears in 20% of resolutions in the founding era and 96% since 2022. "Acting under Chapter VII" went from about 1% of resolutions before 1988 to 50%.The vocabulary of war changed"Aggression" peaked in 1975 to 1987, mostly about South Africa, then all but disappeared. "Breach of the peace" was found for only four wars, the last in 1990. "Threat to the peace" became the routine trigger: 2% of resolutions in the founding era, 55% today.The veto map flipped twiceThe USSR cast most vetoes until 1960, the United States from the 1970s to the 1990s, Russia and China since 2011. 270 drafts have been vetoed since 1946.Unity rose and is now fallingUnanimous adoption climbed from 39% in the founding years to 93% in 2001 to 2010, then fell to 61% in 2025. On contested votes the US and Russia now agree 8% of the time, against 57% around 1990.From wars between states to wars inside themCivilians, women, children and sexual violence were almost absent before 1999. Women now appear in 59% of resolutions and civilians in 38%. The median resolution grew from 234 words in 1960 to 1974 to 1,865 in 2011 to 2021.Africa took over the agendaAfrica went from 0% of resolutions in the founding era to 52% in 2011 to 2021.New agendas and toolsWhen each theme now treated as routine first entered the texts.

Security Council Record is an independent record of every resolution, vote and veto of the United Nations Security Council since 1946. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the United Nations. For official documents, use the Security Council website and the UN Digital Library.

Built on the documentation of the Security Council, the CR-UNSC corpus (Fobbe, Gasbarri and Ridi, CC0), the UN machine-readable resolutions and the UNSC votes since 1946 database (Sciences Po Atelier de cartographie and GRAM, CC BY 4.0). Method and sources.

Made by Daniel D'Esposito with Claude. About this project. Data and code are open. Free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit. Designed to work on any phone and with screen readers.
